notes.meaning: "In those days" means while Jesus was still living quietly at Nazareth. That was many years after the events of chapter 2. John was called "the Baptist" because baptizing people was the mark of his work. He came like a royal herald, calling out God's message in public. The "wilderness of Judea" was rough, thinly settled hill country with some villages in it, not an empty desert.

To "repent" means more than feeling sorry. It is a change of mind and heart that leads to a changed life. "The kingdom of heaven" is God's rule through his promised King, the Messiah. It is a spiritual kingdom that begins on earth and is completed in heaven. The news that it was near was meant to move people to turn back to God, who offers to forgive.

differ.view: "Near" means the kingdom had drawn close but had not yet arrived. A visible kingdom on earth, a thousand-year reign of Christ, is still to come.

notes.meaning: Matthew quotes Isaiah 40:3, which first spoke of God bringing his people home from exile in Babylon. Now it points to John. Servants once went ahead of a king to level roads and clear the way. In the same way, John got people ready for Jesus by calling them to turn from sin and pride. In Isaiah, "the Lord" is God himself, and here the words are applied to Jesus.

John dressed in rough camel's-hair cloth with a leather belt, like the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). Locusts were insects the Law allowed as clean food, and wild honey came from wild bees. His plain, self-denying life matched his call to turn from sin. It also showed that Christ's kingdom is not about worldly show.

Great crowds came from Jerusalem and from all over the countryside. "All" means very many people, not every single person. It was a time of great hope that God was about to act. Yet many who came out of curiosity did not stay faithful later.

The people openly admitted their sins and took the blame on themselves. Baptism, a washing with water, was a sign of being cleansed from sin and of being ready to welcome the coming King. Jews already baptized people from other nations who joined their faith. But baptizing Jews themselves was new and startling.

differ.view: John put people fully under the water. Being immersed pictures the new life of one who has turned to God, and dying and rising with Christ.
Such huge crowds were more likely baptized by water poured on their heads, which pictured the Spirit being poured out. Both dipping and sprinkling are true baptism.
The word does not require full immersion, and the New Testament never commands only one way of baptizing.

notes.meaning: The Pharisees were strict about outward religious rules and proud of their own goodness. The Sadducees denied angels, the resurrection and life after death. Calling them a "brood of vipers" meant they were poisonous under a fine surface. John suspected they came for show, not from real sorrow. "The coming wrath" is God's righteous anger against sin, which falls fully at the final judgment.

differ.view: The "coming wrath" here mainly means the disaster that fell on the Jewish nation when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem.

notes.meaning: "Fruit" means actions that show repentance is real. Repentance lives in the heart like a root, and it shows itself in a changed life, as a tree shows its fruit. Saying sorry while carrying on in the same sins is not true repentance.

Many trusted that being born a child of Abraham would save them. John warns that family line, godly parents or church membership cannot save anyone who does not repent. He may have pointed to the stones nearby. God could make children for Abraham out of them, so he will never lack a people. Many see here a hint that God would call people from other nations.

An axe lying at the root means the tree is about to be cut down, not just trimmed. God's judgment was close. Each person would be tested by the way they lived, not by birth or outward show. Those with no good fruit face the fire of God's judgment.

John could only give the outward sign of washing with water. Christ alone gives the real inner cleansing by the Holy Spirit. Carrying a master's sandals was a job for the lowest slave, so John is saying he is not even worthy to be Jesus' servant. "Fire" pictures the Spirit's work of purifying, warming and burning away sin, as seen at Pentecost.

differ.view: The "fire" means judgment on those who refuse to repent. Some will receive the Spirit, and the unrepentant will face fire, as the next verse describes.

notes.meaning: A winnowing fork tossed grain into the air so the wind blew the light chaff away. The threshing floor stands for God's visible people, where true and false believers are mixed together. The wheat is true believers, whom Christ will gather safely into heaven. The chaff is empty, false believers (hypocrites), who will face the fire that never goes out at the last judgment.

After nearly thirty quiet years in Galilee, the time set by the Father had come. Jesus chose to travel all the way to the Jordan to be baptized by John. It was his first public step, and a humble one.

John tried to stop Jesus. He saw that Jesus was sinless and needed no cleansing, while John himself needed the Spirit-baptism only Christ can give. His words show deep humility, like Peter later saying, "Lord, are you going to wash my feet?"

"Fulfill all righteousness" means doing everything God has commanded, including the baptism God had sent John to give. In this way Jesus approved John's work and fully obeyed his Father. He also shared baptism with his people, so they could have it in common with him. John humbly obeyed.

Heaven opened, and the Holy Spirit came down in a visible form like a dove and rested on Jesus. Jesus did not lack the Spirit before. This openly marked him out and empowered him for his public work as the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2). The dove pictures purity, gentleness and peace.

differ.view: "Went up out of the water" shows that Jesus had been fully immersed.
The wording means he went up "from the water". It does not prove he went under the water.

notes.meaning: The Father's voice declared Jesus to be his beloved Son, in whom he delights, echoing Isaiah 42:1. It was a public sign that Jesus is the promised Messiah. Here the Father speaks, the Son is baptized and the Spirit descends, showing the Trinity: one God in three persons. Because God is pleased with his Son, he also accepts all who belong to Christ by faith.
